judge_assessment.explanation: I re-derived all ten parabolas independently and every feature in answer_key.pdf is right: 1 vertex (3,-4) axis x=3 opens up; 2 vertex (-2,5) axis x=-2 y-intercept 1 opens down; 3 axis -b/2a = -2, vertex (-2,-9), y-intercept -5; 4 zeros -2 and 4, axis midway at x=1, vertex (1,-9); 5 vertex (1,-8), 2(x-1)^2 = 8 gives zeros -1 and 3, a = 2 so narrower; 6 axis 3, vertex (3,4) a maximum since a < 0, y-intercept -5; 7 zeros -3 and 3, vertex (0,-9), axis the y-axis because b = 0; 8 vertex (-4,-2), (x+4)^2 = 4 gives zeros -6 and -2, a = 1/2 so wider, opens up; 9 2(x-1)(x-5) gives zeros 1 and 5, axis 3, vertex (3,-8); 10 y = a(x+1)(x-5) with the point (2,9) forces a(3)(-3) = 9 so a = -1, giving y = -x^2 + 4x + 5, vertex (2,9), opens down. The judge's item-10 claim and its 'quick answers are terse, but the complete worked key is accurate' both hold exactly. What the judge scored as terseness I think has a sharper cause, and there is a second finding the judge did not reach. First, the terseness: the bank prints '1. -4' for a problem asking for a vertex, an axis and an opening direction, and '2. 5, 1' for one asking for a vertex, an axis, a y-intercept and a direction. That is not a formatting choice - the bank is generated from verify.json, and verify.json declares only y-values, so the h-coordinate of every vertex, the equation of every axis, and every up/down and narrower/wider judgement are absent from the verification data entirely. Second, and more consequential: the axis of symmetry is never independently checked anywhere in the file. Entry id 3 is an eval of x**2 + 4*x - 5 AT x = -2 expecting -9. That confirms the height at a number the author chose; it does not confirm that -b/2a is -2. The same shape holds for ids 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 - a mis-derived axis would carry the wrong height through and still verify, because the check evaluates the author's own answer. Third, the worksheet directions require a sketch with a marked vertex, a dashed axis line and plotted intercepts on EVERY problem's grid, and only problem 10 carries a manual entry; nine drawn responses are recorded as machine-verified.

strengths_to_preserve: All ten grids are identical in size and scale (-6 to 6 horizontally, -10 to 10 vertically) and the directions say so on purpose: 'Each grid below is the same size and is blank on purpose - it is your plotting space.' That makes width directly comparable across problems, which is what lets 2(x-1)^2 - 8 in problem 5 and (1/2)(x+4)^2 - 2 in problem 8 be read as narrower and wider against the same reference rather than against a memorised rule.

The sheet is built as three routes to the same four features - vertex form (1, 2, 5, 8), the -b/2a formula (3, 6), and the intercept midpoint (4, 7, 9) - and problem 9 explicitly asks the student to run two of them against each other: 'get the vertex from the midpoint of those intercepts. Check your axis against x = -b/2a'. That is the design that makes it concept practice rather than ten repetitions.

The three declared traps are the sign errors this topic actually produces and each is attached to the problem that provokes it: reading h straight off (x-3)^2 as -3 on problem 1, using +b/2a on problem 3, and dropping the minus on a when computing the axis of -x^2 + 6x - 5 on problem 6. Each trap value (32, 7, -32) is a computed number rather than a hand-typed guess.

Problem 10 is the only genuinely open item and it is the only one carrying a manual entry, whose desc names all five things the sketch must label plus the required sentence - a usable hand-grading instruction rather than 'verify visually'.

root_causes.description: Every feature this worksheet asks for except the vertex height and the zeros is verified indirectly or not at all. The verification pattern is to evaluate the function at the x-coordinate the author already believes is the axis, which makes the check circular with respect to that coordinate: it can catch an arithmetic slip in the height but never a mis-derived axis. Categorical answers (opens up or down, narrower or wider than y = x^2, maximum or minimum) have no representable type at all in the current schema, so they are simply absent, and the Quick Answers bank - which is generated from the same file - inherits the gap and prints unlabelled y-values for multi-feature questions.
evidence: verify.json id 3 is {type: eval, expr: x**2 + 4*x - 5, at: {x: -2}, expected: -9} with the axis stated only in a note field ('Axis x = -b/(2a) = -2'); a note is not a check. The same pattern holds for ids 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10.
worksheet.pdf problems 1, 2 and 3 each print 'Write the vertex and the axis of symmetry'; no entry in verify.json has an axis equation or a vertex x-coordinate as its expected value.

worksheet.pdf problem 5 asks 'Is this parabola narrower or wider than y = x^2?', problem 6 asks 'Is the vertex a maximum or a minimum, and why?', problem 8 asks 'narrower or wider ... and which way does it open?' - none of these have entries.
answer_key.pdf Quick Answers reads '1. -4', '2. 5, 1', '3. -9, -5', '6. 4, -5' - single or paired y-values for four-part questions, which is the judge's answer_key_quality dock made concrete.
The worksheet directions require a sketch on all ten grids; verify.json declares exactly one manual entry, under id 10.

improvements.title: Verify the axis and vertex x-coordinate directly instead of evaluating at the answer, and cover the categorical feature slots
improvements.proposed_change: Replace the circular pattern 'eval f at the presumed axis' with an independent derivation the verifier performs itself: add an entry type that solves for the axis from the coefficients (for standard form, a solve of 2*a*x + b = 0 for the vertex abscissa; for intercept-based items, an entry asserting the axis equals the mean of the two verified zeros) and keep the existing height eval as a second entry under the same id. Add a categorical entry type - a compare of the leading coefficient against 0 for opening direction, and against 1 in absolute value for narrower or wider - so 'opens down' and 'wider than y = x^2' become checked results rather than prose. Then extend the slot inventory so each printed feature request must bind to an entry, which forces all of the above and populates the bank.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: curr-281's problem 3 - prose 'Use x = -b/2a to find the axis of symmetry, then give the vertex and the y-intercept' - with a deliberately corrupted verify.json declaring the axis at x = 2 and an eval expecting x**2 + 4*x - 5 at x = 2 = 7. Under today's contract that file verifies clean (7 is genuinely the value at 2). The new axis-derivation entry must make it fail, and restoring x = -2 with expected -9 must make it pass. Additionally assert the rendered bank row for problem 3 reads with labels covering axis, vertex and y-intercept rather than the bare '-9, -5'.
improvements.expected_impact: Closes a verification hole that is invisible today: eight of the ten problems could carry a wrong axis and still pass every gate. It also fills the Quick Answers bank, which is the judge's stated reason for the answer_key_quality dock, without any change to the worked solutions.
improvements.risk: Deriving the axis inside the verifier requires parsing the quadratic's coefficients, which is straightforward for the polynomial forms on this sheet but will need a clear failure mode (declare manual) for any expression the parser cannot put in standard form; a silent wrong derivation would be worse than the current gap.

improvements.title: Declare manual entries for the nine required sketches, not only problem 10's
improvements.proposed_change: Fail the build when a worksheet problem prints a grid and its directions require a drawing (sketch, mark the vertex, draw the axis as a dashed line, plot the intercepts) but the matching id carries no manual entry. Add nine manual entries here, each desc naming the picture concretely in the style problem 10 already uses - for example, problem 5: a narrow upward V-shaped parabola with vertex (1,-8), dashed axis x = 1, crossing at (-1,0) and (3,0). The directions block that mandates the sketch is printed once at the top of the sheet, so the gate must read the worksheet's directions region as applying to every problem, not just per-problem prose.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture: a worksheet whose global directions block says 'then sketch the curve on its grid, marking the vertex, drawing the axis of symmetry as a dashed vertical line' and whose ten problem ids carry only eval and zeros entries. The gate must exit non-zero listing the nine ids with grids and no manual entry, and must pass once each carries one.
improvements.expected_impact: Gives the teacher the list of ten sketches to look at rather than one, which on a concept-models sheet is the majority of the assessable work. It also removes the current asymmetry where problem 10's identical drawing task is flagged and the other nine are not.
improvements.risk: Directions stated once and applying to all problems are harder to bind than per-problem prose; a naive implementation would flag every problem on any sheet whose header mentions sketching. The gate should require both a global drawing instruction and a per-problem grid or figure to fire.

improvements.title: Label each value in a multi-feature Quick Answers row with the feature it answers
improvements.proposed_change: Have render_quick_answers.py emit a short caption with each value when a problem contributes more than one entry, taken from a new per-entry slot field (vertex, axis, y-int, zeros, opens, width). Row 2 would read 'vertex (-2,5); axis x = -2; y-int 1; opens down' instead of '5, 1'. Where a problem contributes one entry but the prose requests several features, the slot-coverage gate above will have already forced the missing entries, so the label change and the coverage change land together.
improvements.regression_test: Feed render_quick_answers.py curr-281's verify.json and assert row 2 is not the bare '5, 1' and that each printed value carries its feature caption. The assertion fails on today's renderer, which joins expecteds with commas in file order.
improvements.expected_impact: Directly addresses the judge's stated reason for docking answer_key_quality to 3. A teacher can grade a class set from page 1 of the key instead of paging through ten worked solutions to find which number is the vertex height.
improvements.risk: Captioned rows are much wider and will drop the adaptive column count to two on feature-rich sheets, lengthening the key's first page; the renderer needs a width guard or a stacked fallback.

case_summary: Excellent multi-representation parabola practice whose mathematics I confirmed in full - all ten vertices, axes, intercept sets and opening directions re-derive correctly, including problem 10's a = -1 from the point (2,9). The three-route design (vertex form, -b/2a, intercept midpoint) with problem 9 cross-checking two routes against each other, and the ten identically scaled grids that make width comparable across problems, are both worth keeping. The defect the judge sensed as terse Quick Answers has a deeper cause: verify.json declares only y-values, so the vertex x-coordinate, the axis equation and every categorical feature (opens up or down, narrower or wider, maximum or minimum) are outside verification entirely, and the bank has nothing to print for them. Worse, the axis is checked circularly - id 3 evaluates the function AT x = -2 rather than deriving -b/2a - so a mis-derived axis would carry its own wrong height through and still pass. And the directions mandate a sketch on all ten grids while only problem 10 is flagged manual. The ACCEPT stands; the verification contract does not.
